A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EIGN research, with matching authors, problem formulation, and benchmark suite. Their main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-task experiments, traffic-flow evaluations, electrical-circuit simulations, and component ablations, including numerical results and confidence intervals in Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 reports original results on the retained benchmarks, revised model comparisons, and additional sensitivity, architecture, and model-capacity experiments in Appendix E.

M1.justification: v1 propagates signals through fixed Laplacians followed by learned projections. v2 inserts learnable node transformations between boundary maps, replacing propagation with B_out^H h(B_in X). Appendix D.3 implements h as a one-layer MLP for inter-modality propagation and identity mappings within modalities. This substantively changes EIGN's computation; Appendix E.1 also introduces GCN-like and Chebyshev variants.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate RW Comp, LD Cycles, Tri-Flow, the same four traffic networks, and electrical circuits, retaining denoising, interpolation, and simulation tasks. The additional experiments vary architectures and hyperparameters within this coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds LINE-MAGNET and an adapted Dir-GNN to the retained five baselines in the synthetic and real-world comparisons (Tables 4–5 and 9–14). These introduce materially different direction-aware comparators, including a Dir-GNN adaptation satisfying both joint orientation desiderata.

E3.justification: v1 specifies 40/10/50 train/validation/test splits for denoising and 70/10/20 for interpolation and simulation. v2 specifies 80/10/10 for traffic and 50/25/25 for circuits across all three tasks. It also adds a traffic source/sink indicator and keeps associated boundary edges in training (Appendix D.1; Table 8). New capacity controls evaluate four-layer, width-80 baselines.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained direction and fusion ablations, v2 tests removal of the node transformation h (Tables 6 and 15), phase-shift sensitivity (Figure 7), learning rate, width and depth (Table 16), alternative convolution operators, and approximately parameter-matched larger baselines (Table 17). These substantially broaden the tests of design choices and competing explanations.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 20 data splits per hyperparameter configuration, final averages over 50 splits/runs, and 95% confidence intervals for the mean. Additional rows and changed interval values do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Results change throughout the comparison and ablation tables. Reported EIGN Tri-Flow RMSE changes from 0.036 to 0.022, while circuit simulation RMSE changes from 0.583 to 0.696. These are revised results under changed architecture/settings, not controlled performance gains or losses. Table 10's mean-RMSE rankings change from four EIGN denoising wins to one; new comparators and sensitivity experiments add substantial results.

T1.justification: Lemmas 4.1–4.3 and Appendix A generalize orientation and permutation guarantees from linear Laplacian propagation to propagation containing arbitrary node transformations h. New Lemma A.11 proves the zero-output restriction on undirected edges when inter-modality propagation is omitted and equivariant inputs are zero. Appendix E.1 also defines the new convolution variants mathematically.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain joint orientation desiderata, EIGN, and benchmarking. The abstract reframes novelty from the first general-purpose topological GNN handling the combined setting to the first work discussing that setting. The advertised maximum simulation RMSE reduction changes from 43.5% to 23.5%.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of phase-shift ambiguity and the conservative q choice, interprets capacity-controlled comparisons as evidence for inductive biases, and identifies missing communication between edge categories in its Dir-GNN adaptation. It also introduces a node-potential interpretation of propagation and qualifies magnetic Laplacians as one possible realization of the desiderata.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds concrete specifications for LINE-MAGNET, the adapted Dir-GNN, and EIGN's node MLP, including eigenvector counts, layer counts, and dimensions. It documents traffic boundary-feature construction and boundary-map normalization. Appendix E specifies alternative filters and larger-baseline configurations, while Table 17 reports parameter counts. The printed code-access pointer also changes.

R1.justification: v2 acknowledges concurrent Lecha et al. work as an exception to earlier directionality limitations, while distinguishing its treatment of mixed signal modalities. It credits unsigned boundary operators to Bodnar et al. and Papillon et al., and adds Battaglia and Defferrard references for new comparisons and variants. The broader literature framing remains intact.

P1.justification: The seven-section main narrative is retained, with targeted rewrites of the introduction, related work, method explanation, and limitations. A new explanatory Appendix B expands the orientation discussion, shifting the previous Appendices B–D to C–E. The publication header changes and acknowledgements are removed, without wholesale restructuring.

P2.justification: Comparison tables gain baseline rows, and Tables 6 and 15 gain a node-transformation ablation column. v2 adds the three-panel phase-sensitivity Figure 7 and Tables 16–17 for hyperparameters, parameter counts, and variants. Figure 3 updates its convolution labels; the existing conceptual diagrams and Laplacian Table 7 are retained.

improvement.justification: The added direction-aware comparisons and approximate parameter-count controls address important gaps in v1's evidence for EIGN's inductive biases. Generalized proofs and targeted sensitivity and component tests substantially strengthen support for the revised architecture. These benefits outweigh a reporting regression: Appendix E retains the claim of four denoising wins although Table 10 shows only one. Changed architectures and splits prevent treating cross-version score differences as controlled performance improvements.
